query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are not based on the conventional Nb–Ta or Ti-rich families, the superconducting critical temperature (Tc) is set primarily by the average valence-electron concentration (VEC) of the random solid-solution lattice: Tc rises as VEC approaches ≈5.5 e⁻/atom and falls when VEC deviates appreciably from this value because (i) the electronic density of states at the Fermi level is maximised and (ii) the longitudinal acoustic phonon frequency remains high enough for strong BCS-type electron–phonon coupling without excessive disorder scattering.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase body-centred-cubic (BCC) refractory-metal HEA: (Nb₀.₂Ta₀.₂V₀.₂Mo₀.₂W₀.₂) with VEC ≈ 5.0 e⁻/atom; Tc ≈ 4 K (baseline).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary composition along the tie-line (Nb₁₋xTa₁₋xV₀.₂Mo₀.₂W₀.₂+x) to move the average VEC from 4.8 to 6.2 e⁻/atom while preserving single-phase BCC solid-solution character.
generation.conditions: Arc-melt and homogenise ingots under Ar atmosphere; measure resistivity and heat capacity upon cooling from 10 K to 0.3 K at ambient pressure.
generation.structural_mediator: Random BCC solid solution whose lattice parameter contracts modestly as VEC increases, affecting the electronic density of states and Debye temperature.
generation.mechanism: BCS electron–phonon superconductivity in a chemically disordered lattice; tuning VEC toward ≈5.5 e⁻/atom raises N(EF) while maintaining high phonon frequencies, maximising the McMillan λ and hence Tc. Deviation from this VEC lowers Tc because either N(EF) or λ decrease and/or disorder scattering increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with 5.4 ≤ VEC ≤ 5.6 e⁻/atom will exhibit the highest Tc (≈7–8 K), roughly doubling the baseline Tc of the equiatomic starting alloy (≈4 K). Tc will decrease for VEC <5.2 or >5.8, forming an approximately bell-shaped Tc(VEC) curve.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic (NbTaVMoW) HEA with VEC ≈5.0 e⁻/atom showing Tc ≈4 K and a Sommerfeld coefficient γ₀ ≈ 6 mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻².
generation.boundary: Relationship expected to hold only while (a) the alloy remains a single-phase BCC solid solution (confirmed by XRD and SEM-EDS) and (b) measurements are at ambient pressure; long-range ordering, second-phase precipitation, or pressures >2 GPa may invalidate the trend.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of Tc enhancement is uncertain (±1 K) because actual electron–phonon coupling strength and disorder scattering rates are not yet measured; unforeseen magnetic impurities could suppress Tc.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare at least seven compositions spanning VEC 4.8 to 6.2 e⁻/atom in ≈0.2-e⁻ steps, confirm single-phase BCC structure, and measure Tc by four-probe resistivity and heat-capacity jump ΔC/γTc.
measurements: Sommerfeld coefficient γ (from C/T vs T²)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Tc does not exhibit a maximum within VEC = 5.4–5.6 e⁻/atom, or if Tc varies monotonically with VEC, the hypothesis that Tc is controlled chiefly by proximity to VEC ≈5.5 e⁻/atom is falsified.
